findings.title: Validator has a side effect: it updates match_count on every validation
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record each time it is called. It is called from a validator that runs on every `valid?`/`save`. In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` runs and then `user.save` runs validations again, so each signup attempt counts twice. It also writes to the database from inside validation, which is unexpected and inflates the statistics.

findings.title: Email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` is an exact match. A blocked address can be bypassed by changing the case (Spam@x.com vs spam@x.com) or adding whitespace. The email is not downcased on lookup or on storage. Also, `value` can be nil, which would query `email IS NULL`.

findings.title: Racy read-modify-write of match_count
findings.body: `match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a lost-update race under concurrent signups. It also skips the model's own validations and callbacks when saving. Use an atomic `update_all`/`increment_counter` instead.

findings.title: Naming the validator EmailValidator may collide with other validators and does not handle nil values
findings.body: The class name `EmailValidator` can shadow or collide with other email validators (for example, a gem's). `email_in_restriction_setting?` and `should_block?` are called with `value`, which may be nil. The user model's `presence` validation also runs, but the whitelist `=~` on nil silently flags the record as not allowed.

findings.title: Shared mutable array on controller prototype
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the class prototype, so all instances of the controller share one array. Rejected emails persist across instances. Initialize it in `init` instead.
